beats.narration_text: Merhaba — this is Liam, in for Bear. Mickey’s building a final project that looks inside a national financial stress index. The question is genuinely good: one headline number collapses credit markets, bank funding, interest rates, volatility, leverage, and investor risk appetite into a single figure. What’s actually inside, and which parts matter most? The trouble isn’t the ambition. It’s that the index construction makes clean attribution structurally hard before any model runs. Here is what Professor Bear would say.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Merhaba, Liam'; ask types itself
running indicator 'reading the index… stress-testing the methods…'

props.command: What feedback would Professor Bear give Mickey on their Computational Skepticism final project?
props.runningText: reading the index… stress-testing the methods…
output: The question is good. The index construction makes it harder than it looks.
Three methods, three documented failure modes — and one runs through all of them.
Here’s what to build in before it goes under review.

beats.narration_text: Act one. Mickey’s project, and the structural trap inside a good question.

lines: Mickey’s Ambition

beats.narration_text: One headline stress number collapses very different things into a single figure. Mickey wants to look inside: which component matters most, and when? Three methods — contribution analysis, machine learning, topological data analysis — each attacking the question from a different angle. The toolkit is ambitious and well-matched to a doctoral project in finance.

shot.pantry_brief: abstract financial dashboard: a single bold index line above a fan of six faint coloured sub-components; warm ink on cream; minimal, no real institution logos — Tier 1 illustrative

lines: One number, six very different drivers

build.suggested: suggested prompt: One headline stress number collapses very different things into a single figure. Mickey wants to look inside: which component matters most, and when? Three meth

beats.narration_text: The toolkit is ambitious and well-matched. The trouble isn’t the ambition — it’s that all three methods share one structural constraint before they start: their inputs are the same highly correlated components.

lines: Ambitious and well-matched — with one shared constraint.
Contribution analysis — which component explains the most variance?
Machine learning — does importance shift during crisis episodes?

beats.narration_text: And in a crisis, everything correlates to one. Credit spreads move with volatility, which moves with funding stress. The components that the index decomposes are themselves entangled — which means any attribution method inherits that entanglement before it starts.

manim.spec: Three labeled method boxes (CONTRIBUTION | ML | TDA) arranged in a row at top; below them, six input component bars (CREDIT | FUNDING | RATES | VOL | LEVERAGE | RISK) connected to each method box by lines; correlation lines animate between the input bars during 'crisis' highlight, glowing terracotta, converging toward a single line labeled r≈0.9; the entanglement is the visual, not a mistake

lines: In a crisis — everything correlates to one

beats.narration_text: Act two. The attribution problem is structural, not a modeling choice.

lines: No Unique Decomposition

beats.narration_text: Take two correlated inputs — credit spreads and volatility, correlated at 0.9 during a crisis. SHAP values might report each at forty percent importance. That adds up to eighty because they’re sharing credit. The real honest statement: these two are so entangled here that individual attribution is not meaningful.

manim.spec: Two vertical bars side by side: CREDIT SPREAD and VOLATILITY; an r=0.9 correlation arc connects them; SHAP reports each at ~40% in a bar chart below; a terracotta question mark appears over the 80% total with annotation 'attribution ill-posed'; the bars blur/smear into each other to show entanglement

lines: Each 40% — entangled, not additive

beats.narration_text: When inputs are collinear, there is no single correct decomposition of how much each contributed. SHAP, regression decomposition, LMG — they give different answers. Not because one is wrong, but because they encode different definitions of contribution under collinearity.

shot.pantry_brief: correlation matrix heatmap of six financial stress components, warm terracotta tones in the high-correlation cells; a statistical artifact, not a real index — Tier 1 illustrative

show.event: correlation matrix visible, slow drift inward on the high-correlation cluster
terracotta underline under ‘different definitions of contribution’

lines: Different definitions — different answers

build.suggested: suggested prompt: When inputs are collinear, there is no single correct decomposition of how much each contributed. SHAP, regression decomposition, LMG — they give different answ

beats.narration_text: The feedback: lead with the multicollinearity diagnostic before any attribution analysis. A VIF that spikes during crises is itself a finding — direct evidence that which indicator matters most is least well-posed exactly when you care about it most.

shot.pantry_brief: VIF time-series chart for a financial stress component, 2005-2023, showing dramatic spikes at 2008 and 2020; clean axes, warm ink on cream — Tier 1 illustrative

show.event: plate holds at A2V1 handoff camera position, pans to VIF chart
terracotta ring draws on the 2008 spike — ‘this is the finding’

lines: The spike is the finding

build.suggested: suggested prompt: The feedback: lead with the multicollinearity diagnostic before any attribution analysis. A VIF that spikes during crises is itself a finding — direct evidence

beats.narration_text: Here’s what that looks like. VIF for a typical stress-index component in calm periods: two or three. VIF at the 2008 and 2020 crisis peaks: fifteen, twenty, higher. The spike marks exactly where attribution is most requested — and least reliable.

manim.spec: Time series 2005-2023 of a VIF value (stylized, not real data); calm-period baseline at ~2-3 drawn first; crisis period shading blocks appear at 2008 and 2020; VIF line spikes sharply to 15-20 within those blocks; terracotta vertical markers at crisis peaks; annotation ‘attribution least reliable here’ with hairline pointer; horizontal dashed threshold at VIF=10 (conventional multicollinearity warning)

lines: Calm: 2-3. Crisis peak: 15-20.

beats.narration_text: Run SHAP and regression decomposition on the same crisis window. Different indicator rankings, both internally consistent. Neither is wrong — they’re answering different questions. Pick one definition and justify it, or run both and report the disagreement as the finding.

left.label: SHAP — marginal contribution
left.note: distributes credit ‘fairly’ by average marginal impact; correlated features share credit

right.label: REGRESSION DECOMP — partial variance
right.note: attributes variance after partialing out others; different ranking under collinearity

beats.narration_text: SHAP asks: how much does this feature shift the prediction on average, holding the others to their marginal distribution? Regression decomposition asks: how much variance does this explain when I partial out the others? Different questions, different answers — both are legitimate.

manim.spec: Two card panels side by side: LEFT labeled SHAP, terracotta header; a short math-flavored phrase ‘E[Δf | x_i]’ (not rendered as LaTeX, just text); below it the question in plain text. RIGHT labeled REGRESSION DECOMP; similar structure with partial-variance language. Between the panels a clean vertical divider. Neither has a ‘wrong’ marker — both get equal visual weight. Bottom annotation: ‘Pick one. Justify it. Or report both.’

lines: Pick one and justify it — or report both

beats.narration_text: Act three. How many independent crisis episodes does ‘importance changes during crises’ actually need to establish? The modern era offers an uncomfortable answer.

lines: Three Episodes

props.command: render a Manim scene: a 2005–2025 time axis with three crisis blocks marked — GFC 2008, COVID 2020, Rate Shock 2022 — and a sample-size annotation N≈3 visible

beats.narration_text: The modern-era sample: 2008, 2020, arguably 2022. Three crisis episodes, maybe four if you count generously. A model that finds crisis-specific importance patterns is estimating those patterns on three data points, however sophisticated its architecture.

manim.spec: Horizontal time axis 2005-2025; three shaded crisis blocks appear sequentially: GFC 2008, COVID 2020, Rate Shock 2022; each block labeled; above the timeline a count annotation increments: N=1, N=2, N=3; final annotation reads ‘N≈3 independent episodes’ in terracotta; the sparseness of the blocks vs the long calm periods is the visual point

lines: Importance on ≈3 independent episodes

beats.narration_text: Crisis-period importance estimates have very high variance. Shift the window definition by one month either direction — if the indicator ranking reorders, that instability is the result. Report it as a limitation, not a modeling detail. And ask honestly: with three episodes, is there meaningful out-of-sample validation?

shot.pantry_brief: a crisis-window diagram: a time segment with a shaded block and dotted boundary lines showing ±1-month perturbation; two indicator ranking bars shown as reordered under the shift; warm ink on cream, no real data — Tier 1 illustrative

lines: If the ranking reorders — that IS the finding

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Crisis-period importance estimates have very high variance. Shift the window definition by one month either direction — if the indicator ranking reorders, that

beats.narration_text: The required robustness check: perturb the crisis-window boundaries by plus or minus one month, recompute the importance ranking, and report explicitly whether the ordering holds. If it doesn’t, that’s the limitation section writing itself.

props.title: ML Section: Four Robustness Requirements
chips: Perturb crisis-window boundaries ±1 month — does ranking hold?
Report instability explicitly — not smoothed in a limitation footnote
Out-of-sample protocol — what’s the hold-out given N≈3 episodes?
Validate the pattern, not just the model’s in-sample fit

beats.narration_text: The three-episode constraint isn’t a reason to abandon the ML approach. It’s a reason to report its bounds honestly. A finding that survives boundary perturbation and a stated out-of-sample protocol is a real finding. One that doesn’t report those checks is a target for reviewers.

props.title: From N≈3 to a Defensible Finding
props.note: boundary-stable ranking + stated out-of-sample protocol = defensible
props.sparkLine: Report the bounds — don’t smooth them.

beats.narration_text: Act four. Topological data analysis is legitimate on financial time series. But persistence diagrams have a documented failure mode on this kind of data.

lines: The Parameter Artifact

beats.narration_text: Persistence diagrams are highly sensitive to preprocessing choices — embedding dimension, window length, distance metric, filtration range. Run the same financial stress data through four parameter combinations. You get four different topological signatures, each visually distinct. One will look like the best story.

manim.spec: 2×2 grid of small persistence diagram sketches (abstract scatter plots of dots at varying (birth, death) positions); each labeled with its parameter combination (dim=2 win=20; dim=3 win=20; dim=2 win=40; dim=3 win=40); the dots differ visibly across panels; a terracotta star marks the ‘cleanest-looking’ one with the annotation ‘this one tells the best story’; caption below: ‘all four are the same data’

lines: Four parameters, four different signatures

beats.narration_text: The threshold question: does the qualitative conclusion — stress becomes topologically concentrated during crises — hold across a range of parameter choices? Or does it appear only under the cleanest-looking combination? That is the difference between a finding and an artifact.

left.label: FINDING
left.note: qualitative conclusion holds across embedding dims and window lengths — the cross-method agreement confirms it

right.label: ARTIFACT
right.note: conclusion appears under one parameter combination; dissolves under the others — a function of the choices, not the data

beats.narration_text: And ask whether the TDA findings cross-validate against the contribution analysis. If Part 1 and Part 3 point in the same direction, convergence is real evidence. If they diverge, investigate. Do not report only the method whose story is more publishable.

shot.pantry_brief: abstract two-panel comparison: LEFT a stylized bar chart (contribution analysis result), RIGHT a stylized persistence diagram; a check-mark convergence symbol in terracotta between them; clean, no real data — Tier 1 illustrative

lines: Convergence is evidence — divergence is a finding

build.suggested: suggested prompt: And ask whether the TDA findings cross-validate against the contribution analysis. If Part 1 and Part 3 point in the same direction, convergence is real evidenc

beats.narration_text: Act five. Descriptive attribution versus causal language — and why the distinction matters under review.

lines: Description vs Causation

beats.narration_text: Two statements about the same index window. Left: credit market stress accounts for forty percent of the index variance in this period. Descriptive — defensible. Right: credit market stress caused the spike. Causal — and none of the three methods support it.

left.label: DESCRIPTIVE — defensible
left.note: ‘Credit stress accounts for 40% of the index variance in this window.’

right.label: CAUSAL — unsupported
right.note: ‘Credit stress caused the spike.’ None of the three methods are causal identification tools.

beats.narration_text: Contribution analysis, SHAP, and topological data analysis all describe statistical association within a constructed index. They are not causal identification tools. Every causal verb in the write-up — drove, caused, triggered, led to — is a reviewer’s target.

manim.spec: A vertical list of four verb pairs, appearing one by one: CAUSED → accounts for | DROVE → is associated with | TRIGGERED → co-moves with | LED TO → corresponds to. Each causal verb is in a light warm-ink colour; as it arrives, a terracotta strikethrough draws across it; the replacement verb fades in beside it in dark INK. Final frame shows all four pairs simultaneously.

lines: Audit the draft — every causal verb is a target

beats.narration_text: Audit the draft for drove, caused, triggered, led to. Wherever the method is descriptive, those words need to go — replaced with accounts for, is associated with, co-moves with. This is not defensive writing. Finance and econometrics reviewers will mark unsupported causal claims as unsubstantiated.

shot.pantry_brief: a draft paper page with four circled phrases in terracotta: ‘drove’, ‘caused’, ‘triggered’, ‘led to’; the body text is illegible lorem-ipsum filler, not real text; editorial markup feel — Tier 1 illustrative

lines: Causal claims need causal methods

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Audit the draft for drove, caused, triggered, led to. Wherever the method is descriptive, those words need to go — replaced with accounts for, is associated wit

beats.narration_text: The causal audit is not defensive writing. It is precision. A decomposition result reported as a decomposition is defensible. Reported as causation, it becomes a retraction target — especially in finance, where reviewers are specifically trained to probe causal claims.

props.title: The Causal Audit: Four Verb Replacements

beats.narration_text: Act six. What honest visualization looks like under collinearity — and the publication argument for building all of this in now.

lines: The Honest Chart

props.command: render a Manim scene: side-by-side comparison of a crisp waterfall attribution chart and a banded/uncertain version of the same chart, communicating collinearity uncertainty

beats.narration_text: The conventional waterfall or stacked-area chart implies a cleanness of separation that collinear inputs do not support. Where VIF shows serious collinearity, communicate uncertainty — banded contributions with explicit ranges, not crisp percentage splits.

manim.spec: Two-panel comparison: LEFT a clean waterfall chart with six stacked blocks labeled with crisp percentages (CREDIT 38%, FUNDING 22%, etc.); RIGHT the same layout but each block replaced by a banded range (e.g., CREDIT 25-50%) with a shaded uncertainty band; the left panel is labeled CONVENTIONAL, the right HONEST UNDER COLLINEARITY; terracotta bracket marks the right panel

lines: Banded, not crisp — under collinearity

beats.narration_text: The cross-method comparison chart should show agreement AND disagreement — explicitly, not cherry-picked. Where SHAP, regression decomposition, and TDA converge, that convergence is your strongest evidence. Where they diverge, that divergence is a finding about the methods themselves.

lines: Show agreement AND disagreement — both are findings.
SHAP + Regression agree: credit dominates in calm periods → convergence = evidence
SHAP + TDA agree on crisis topology → convergence = evidence

beats.narration_text: Persistence diagrams need the parameter-sensitivity result shown alongside the headline — small multiples across a few parameter choices, not one clean diagram. The agreement across the multiples is the evidence. One beautiful diagram with no context is a liability.

manim.spec: A 2×2 grid of persistence diagrams (same data, four parameter sets); each panel has a small label (dim/window); a terracotta agreement band or region visible in a similar position across all four panels; caption: ‘Agreement across all four — the pattern is robust’; a fifth ‘bad example’ shows a single large diagram with no comparison — labeled with a subtle warning marker

lines: Small multiples, not one clean diagram

beats.narration_text: Here is the publication argument for building all of this in now. Reviewers in finance and econometrics will specifically probe collinearity handling and crisis-sample size — these are known entry points in the literature. Building the checks in is not a delay. It is what makes the paper defensible under peer review, not just course-grading.

shot.pantry_brief: abstract peer-review scenario: a manuscript page with two reviewer comment bubbles marked in terracotta — one pointing to a collinearity section, one to a crisis-N table; no real identifiers; editorial feel — Tier 1 illustrative

lines: Build the checks in now — reviewers will probe

build.suggested: suggested prompt: Here is the publication argument for building all of this in now. Reviewers in finance and econometrics will specifically probe collinearity handling and crisis

beats.narration_text: Mickey’s project, three methods, and Bear’s four checkpoints. Lead with the VIF diagnostic — the spike is the finding. Report crisis importance on ≈3 episodes honestly — boundary-test it. Give TDA its own parameter-sensitivity sweep and cross-validate against Part 1. Audit every causal verb. All four protect the publication goal. Build them in, not after.

artifactLines: VIF spike in crises = attribution is ill-posed exactly when you care most
Crisis importance is N≈3 — boundary-test it; report instability as the finding
TDA needs a parameter-sensitivity sweep before publication
Audit every causal verb — none of the three methods support causal claims

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: I am building a financial stress index decomposition project using contribution analysis, machine learning, and topological data analysis. Walk me through one collinearity diagnostic — VIF across crisis subperiods — and show me what an honest banded visualization of the result looks like, compared to the conventional crisp chart.
